Copying Result<T, String> into sk-code: it is a scaffold convention for generated code whose error text is deliberately not compared, so copying it would weaken sk-code's typed-error rule

label: docs/types.md is a per-language source-type to port-type table whose contract is stated up front: bridge reads each exported function's types from the source and writes the port's signature in port.rs from them; the sk-code Rust set has no source-type to Rust-type mapping table at all.

The port error contract is uniform and untyped, Result<T, String> (and in C it returns T), which contradicts sk-code's typed-thiserror P1 rule and its no-anyhow-in-public-API P0 rule on the surface; the scopes differ because port.rs is a generated scaffold whose error text is deliberately not compared, so it is recorded as a scope conflict rather than a sk-code error.

serde_json::Value is the explicit escape hatch for anything the mapping does not know (objects, maps, unions of different types); the sk-code Rust set has zero hits for serde_json::Value, so it has no named fallback boundary type.

'refused' is a first-class outcome: a function whose types cannot be faithfully bridged stays in its source language with the reason printed (TypeScript refuses Function, RegExp, Iterator/Generator; Python refuses Callable, Iterator, Generator, *args, **kwargs and decorators other than @cache/@lru_cache); the sk-code set has zero hits for refused, so it has no keep-it-in-the-original-language verdict.

A defaulted parameter becomes Option<T>, except where the default is a literal Rust can write (a number, true/false or a plain string) in Python, Ruby, PHP and C#, while TypeScript and JavaScript always use Option<T>; the sk-code set has no default-parameter rule.

The mapping table is executable: cargo test --test types_doc checks every row against the mapping so a row that no longer matches the code fails the build, implemented by include_str!("../docs/types.md") and iterating the documented rows against bridge::param_type; the sk-code set has no rule that a documented mapping table must be tested against the implementation, and this is the most portable single rule in the file.

The C ABI keeps width and sign through std::ffi (int to c_int, long to c_long with the note 32 bits on Windows, size_t to usize, ssize_t/ptrdiff_t/intptr_t to isize, float to f32, double to f64, long double and wchar_t refused), with specifiers in any order, const and volatile ignored, enum as c_int and a scalar typedef as that scalar; the sk-code set has zero hits for std::ffi, c_int or c_char, so the C ABI is entirely absent.

C pointers are mapped by their neighbouring parameter (const char* to Option<&[u8]>, a const byte pointer plus an integer length to &[u8] with the length dropped, a writable byte pointer plus a size to &mut [u8], a written scalar pointer to Option<&mut T>, char** into a string parameter to Option<&mut Option<usize>>, a by-value all-scalar struct to #[repr(C)]), and every other pointer is refused with 'ownership must be designed' or 'who frees it must be designed'; the sk-code set has zero hits for repr(C), and the refusal wording is the valuable part because it turns pointer ownership into a design decision.

The integer mapping is per source language rather than global: TypeScript number maps to f64 while Python int maps to i64; sk-code mentions f64 in 18 files and i64 in 3 but never frames the choice as a per-source-language decision, so the JavaScript case is covered implicitly and the Python case is absent.

docs/types.md has no PyO3 section: the Python section maps Python source types to Rust port types and never names PyO3, and PyO3 appears only as the Python bridge in the website docs ('Python | PyO3 (abi3), direct conversion, typed exceptions'); the topic's premise therefore overstates the source, and the honest edit is a PyO3 bridge row in sk-code's interop model rather than a value table.
